Narrator Vira Toland recounts how in 1919 the Ostrey Hollow milk station tester Ansel Keddie was accused of watering cans, causing a lasting rift with his brother-in-law Emmet Brant, until it emerged he'd actually been skimming cream and was ousted after a hearing, leaving lingering shame despite the family's tangled cousin ties to the Association.

This 1966 report doesn't mention 1908 at all — it recommends a levy of six mills on the dollar for 1907, wait, no: it recommends six mills for 1967, so there's no levy figure for 1908 given in this document.

Narrator Effie Loomis, longtime Association secretary, gives a bylaws/record history explaining Article VII's "station test governs" clause and the 1925 arbitration that paid Ostrey Hollow patrons $3,800 "without admission," while flagging gaps in the record—especially the unmentioned 1923 condemned measuring-crate.
The play being performed at the Ellerby Playhouse is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Narrator Ansel Keddie gives sworn testimony and an unsent letter meticulously defending his 29 years of careful testing method, highlighting the unexplained 1911 measure-swap anomaly and insisting he never skimmed cream, even though he was still put out despite "no cause established."
The wholesale order placed with Purcell & Weare on 14 March 1932 totaled $59.65.

Narrator Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, presents forensic proof to a historical society that the station's low milk-fat readings for decades were caused by undersized pipette glassware—not theft or watering—fully exonerating her grandfather long after his death.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Narrator Wilbur Teague, the Association's longtime bookkeeper, explains the "station gain" line showing Ostrey Hollow's credited milk fat was consistently ~5.25% below what actually arrived at Larrow Green, and argues this reflected an unsupervised single-man system ripe for skimming rather than any fixed mystery.
Judge Thurlow Vane's court fined Delia Fought $5.00 for the petty theft of dress goods.

Narrator Merle Strawn, a retired state dairy inspector, presents his dry year-by-year circuit-book entries for Ostrey Hollow, culminating in his 1923 discovery that the station's pipettes were undersized and condemning them, while insisting he records only facts and no opinions.
Lemma 2.1 is named "Interleaving."

Narrator Halbert Nym, museum curator, compiles a 16-item catalogue of primary documents (bylaws, ledgers, the condemned pipette crate, arbitration records) tracing the Ostrey Hollow station's low-test mystery through to its exoneration in Bulletin No. 471.
Mr. Ansgar Krell remained at the Cold Spring Water-Cure for 4 weeks.

Narrator Selby Vose, the Association's manager, defends the 1925 arbitration payout as generous goodwill and insists the station's improved 1924 test figures prove patrons had been watering their milk and stopped once scrutinized—dismissing the condemned testing apparatus as mere routine wear-and-tear, unrelated to the real cause.

Retelling 09 — Roy Brant's 1955 farm bureau account of his father Emmet Brant's milk-weight ledger, showing the scales never lied while confirming the chronic 0.17-point test shortfall at Ostrey Hollow (including the unexplained 1911 anomaly) and the Keddie/Brant family rift from the 1919 circular.
Dr. Pemberton charged $8.00 for the confinement and mileage in Mrs. Content Averill's delivery on January 3, 1906.

Retelling 10 — Rosalie Cudd's 1958 letter to Ivy Keddie, giving the Alder Corners Cheese Company's independent test records (consistently ~3.80) for the four Hessel Bottom farmers who hauled there in summer, corroborating that the Ostrey Hollow milk itself was never actually low-testing.
The man's crown will cost him $1,480 after insurance.

Retelling 11 — Professor Leland Vaught's October 1958 introduction to Bulletin No. 471, explaining the proportional-error physics of a short pipette and reproducing the bulletin's exoneration conclusion — though this account gives figures (16.27 c.c. mean delivery, five dozen pipettes bought, glass entering use "1 May 1898," a 118,000 lb shortfall) that diverge from the same details given in other retellings.
The color named in the third paragraph is vermilion (Bettine Rausch's apron).

Retelling 12 — Dell Rundle's 1939 jubilee pamphlet (reprinted 1959 with a footnote) on the Association's fifty-year history, recounting the folk "cream theft" belief at Ostrey Hollow but appending a late correction (after seeing the ledgers) admitting the station actually delivered *more* fat to Larrow Green than credited, undermining her own chapter IV.
Message No. 219, "FATHER VERY LOW COME AT ONCE," was 6 words.

Retelling 13 — Alonzo Frick's 1946 bar association yearbook recollection as the arbitration board's chairman, describing the three competing (unproven) theories aired at the hearing and Keddie's dismissal four days before the award — plus a private aside that Keddie privately blamed the patrons, complicating his public denial.
The locksmith's dog is a gray terrier named Buckley.

Retelling 14 — Hobart Sill's 1934 retirement remarks as the Larrow Green buttermaker, insisting the Hollow's cream always "ran heavy" (came in with more fat than credited) while nonetheless personally believing the patrons watered their milk — an eyewitness account that unwittingly corroborates the "no cream stolen" finding even as he argues the opposite conclusion.
The norm defined in Definition 1.3 is called the Trebbin norm.

Retelling 15 — Nyle Grigg's 1919 covering letter reprinting his 1908 committee report, defending the "wet hay" theory and citing Bulletin No. 214 as vindication — though his letter's claim of year-round sampling contradicts the report's own text (January–March only), and his cited Bulletin figure ("two tenths") differs from the figure given elsewhere.

Retelling 16 — Dr. Roland Kepp's 1926 farm club paper, a veterinarian's soil-chemistry defense of the wet-hay theory (citing a "two tenths" Bulletin 214 figure that conflicts with the bulletin's actual "five hundredths" wording) who dismisses the 1911 anomaly by misstating its length as six weeks rather than nine.
Phyl warns Armando not to use dryer number eleven.

Hazel Brant (1981 taped interview, Roy Brant's daughter and Ivy Keddie's second cousin) recounts the family weigh-book history, the Keddie family relationships, and the 1899 glassware crate found in the loft that Ivy discovered was the true cause of the chronic 0.19-point shortfall — but gives figures diverging from other sources (station glass arriving 1899 not 1896/1898; condemned in '21 not '23; hearing in '26 not '25; nine letters to nine families on six farms).
The third paragraph names the color magenta (the scarf worn by the woman they called Tuesday).

Duncan Keddie (Ansel's son, retired schoolteacher, 1968 family notes) lays out the Brant-Keddie-Vose family relationships and the provenance of the five key documents/objects (station test book, Brant weigh book, Strawn's notebooks, Alder Corners book, the condemned glassware crate) — but gives the Brant weigh book's start date as 1897 and the crate's move to the loft as 1923, both diverging from r17's 1900 and 1921.
The coroner's jury found that Obadiah Chalmers died by accidental drowning after falling from the flume edge while working, with no evidence of another person's involvement.

*The Ashlin Chronicle* (Oct 3, 1958 front-page feature) recaps the vindication story via Ivy Keddie's telephone interview — but introduces new discrepancies: Rosalie Cudd is called Jerome Cudd's "niece" (not "daughter" as in earlier retellings) and it states eleven measurable pipettes from six dozen bought.
The total ice-out pot in the spring of 1996 was six thousand eight hundred and forty dollars.

Junia Ammon (Ammon & Sons' company historian, 1949 privately printed history) reproduces the firm's original 1897 invoice and its 1923 reply letter, and speculates the pipette mold was reground and ran consistently short by accident — but her invoice total ($77.93) conflicts with the Chronicle's "$77.39" figure, and her station start date (1 May 1897) is a third variant alongside earlier sources' 4 May 1896 and 1 May 1898.
In Proposition 4.1, the sharpness example uses a 7-cycle.

Cleve Oram (cream hauler's son, taped 1977 at Larrow Green) recalls the wagon route, the loft crate he personally handled, and the arbitration hearings — but his figures ($3,500 award, five dozen pipettes/nine surviving, 67,000 lb shortfall) and family claims (Ivy as Hazel's "first cousin once removed," Keddies and Voses "cousins of some sort") directly contradict Duncan Keddie's explicit corrections in r18.

This is Orin Falke's 1959 county-agent report synthesizing the whole Ostrey Hollow question for the board of supervisors — laying out the timeline, refuting the water and cream-theft theories, initially crediting the wet-hay theory, then retracting that concession in an appended note after obtaining Bulletin No. 214's actual figures (0.05 in winter, none in summer, insufficient to explain the 0.19 gap), and correcting Ivy Keddie's relation to Ansel as granddaughter rather than great-niece.
Russ's wife is named Dorrit.

Bertram Kyle (retired Association clerk, 1953 memoir for the Historical Society) describes decades of copying the Ostrey Hollow station accounts, revealing that the "station gain" (cream running heavy) was routinely recorded as an unremarked accounting line ("five and a quarter per cent, as usual") — while also introducing new date discrepancies: pipette condemnation in "twenty-two" (1922) and the arbitration award in "twenty-four" (1924), both earlier than other sources' 1923/1925, though he confirms Selby Vose as Gideon's son (not nephew), matching Duncan Keddie's r18 correction.
The third paragraph names the color teal (the endpapers of the collected edition).

Orra Keddie's diary (1897–1930, published 1964) gives an intimate domestic chronicle of Ansel's tenure and dismissal, the rift with her brother Emmet over the 1919 water circular, and Ansel's quiet dignity after being turned out — but introduces fresh discrepancies: the circular went to "eleven families" (not r17's nine), the station's own glass arrived "May 1, 1897" (a third date, matching r20 but not r02/r11), and she gives her own birth year as 1866 versus Duncan's stated 1868.
The total toll collected at the Wren's Bend bridge for the week of June 5–11, 1899 was $13.88.
